html:
The Curonians were a Baltic people of the coast of what is now western Latvia and Lithuania, known from the 400s to the 1500s CE. The map uses the name earlier, from 500 BCE to 100 CE, for the Baltic peoples of that coast.

They lived from farming, fishing and the sea. In the Viking Age they were seafarers and raiders themselves, sometimes called the "Baltic Vikings". Scandinavians settled among them at Grobiņa in the 600s and 700s, and Swedish and Danish fleets attacked them in the 800s; the Life of Saint Ansgar tells of a Swedish siege of their fort at Apuolė around 854.

In the 1200s German crusaders reached the eastern Baltic. At the Battle of Durbe in 1260 the Curonians in the crusader army switched sides, helping the Samogitians crush the Teutonic Knights and the Livonian Order. By 1267 the Curonians had been conquered and converted. Their land took their name as Courland, and they merged into the Latvian and Lithuanian peoples. Their language died out by the 1600s. The Curonian Spit, the long dune peninsula off Klaipėda, still carries their name.
